notes.definition: Electrolysis is the process in which an electric current is passed through an electrolyte (a molten or dissolved ionic compound), causing the ions to move to the electrodes, where they are discharged to form elements.
explanation: An ionic compound is made of positive and negative ions held in a giant lattice by strong electrostatic forces. In a solid, the ions are fixed in position and can only vibrate, so the solid cannot conduct electricity. When the compound is melted, or dissolved in water, the lattice breaks up and the ions are free to move about within the liquid or solution. Liquids and solutions that conduct electricity because they contain mobile ions are called electrolytes.

For electrolysis, two electrodes are placed in the electrolyte and connected to a direct current (d.c.) power supply. The electrode connected to the positive terminal is the anode, and the electrode connected to the negative terminal is the cathode. Electrodes are often made of graphite or platinum, which conduct electricity and are inert, meaning they do not react with the electrolyte or the products.

When the current flows, opposite charges attract. Positively charged ions (cations), such as metal ions and hydrogen ions, move to the negative electrode, the cathode. Negatively charged ions (anions), such as chloride, bromide and oxide ions, move to the positive electrode, the anode. In the wires and electrodes the current is a flow of electrons, but inside the electrolyte the current is carried by moving ions.

When the ions reach the electrodes they are discharged: they gain or lose electrons and become neutral atoms or molecules of elements. At the cathode, positive ions gain electrons, so metals (or hydrogen) are produced. At the anode, negative ions lose electrons, so non-metals such as chlorine, bromine or oxygen are produced. Overall the compound is broken down (decomposed) into its elements, so electrolysis needs a continuous supply of electrical energy.

Substances that are made of molecules, such as sugar dissolved in water, contain no ions, so they are not electrolytes and cannot be electrolysed. Metals and graphite conduct electricity by delocalised electrons, not ions, so they are conductors but not electrolytes. A useful memory aid is PANIC: Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode.
keyFacts: Ionic compounds conduct when molten or dissolved in water, because the ions are free to move.
Solid ionic compounds do not conduct: the ions are fixed in the lattice.
An electrolyte is a liquid or solution containing ions that are free to move.
The cathode is the negative electrode; the anode is the positive electrode.
Positive ions (cations) move to the cathode; negative ions (anions) move to the anode.
Ions are discharged at the electrodes to form elements.
Electrolysis uses a direct current (d.c.) supply.
Inert electrodes such as graphite or platinum do not react with the electrolyte or products.
In the electrolyte, the current is carried by ions; in the wires, by electrons.

keyTerms.definition: The breaking down of an ionic compound, when molten or in solution, by passing an electric current through it.
A molten or dissolved ionic compound that conducts electricity because its ions are free to move.
A solid conductor, often graphite or platinum, through which current enters or leaves the electrolyte.
The negative electrode, which attracts positive ions.
The positive electrode, which attracts negative ions.
A positively charged ion, such as Na⁺, Cu²⁺ or H⁺.
A negatively charged ion, such as Cl⁻, Br⁻ or O²⁻.
When an ion gains or loses electrons at an electrode to become a neutral atom or molecule.
An electrode that does not react with the electrolyte or the products of electrolysis.

workedExamples.title: Predicting where ions go
workedExamples.question: Molten calcium chloride, CaCl₂, is electrolysed using graphite electrodes. State which ions move to each electrode and name the products.
steps: Identify the ions: calcium chloride contains Ca²⁺ ions and Cl⁻ ions.
Ca²⁺ is positive, so it is attracted to the negative electrode (cathode).
Cl⁻ is negative, so it is attracted to the positive electrode (anode).
At the cathode Ca²⁺ ions gain electrons and form calcium metal.
At the anode Cl⁻ ions lose electrons and form chlorine gas, Cl₂.
workedExamples.answer: Ca²⁺ ions move to the cathode and form calcium; Cl⁻ ions move to the anode and form chlorine gas.

workedExamples.title: Deciding whether a substance is an electrolyte
workedExamples.question: Which of these could be electrolysed: solid sodium chloride, molten sodium chloride, sugar solution, copper sulfate solution?
steps: An electrolyte must contain ions that are free to move.
Solid sodium chloride has ions, but they are fixed in the lattice: not an electrolyte.
Molten sodium chloride has mobile ions: electrolyte.
Sugar is a covalent molecular substance, so its solution has no ions: not an electrolyte.
Copper sulfate solution contains mobile Cu²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions: electrolyte.
workedExamples.answer: Molten sodium chloride and copper sulfate solution can be electrolysed.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think solid ionic compounds conduct electricity because they contain ions.
misconceptions.right: In fact the ions in a solid are fixed in the lattice. They must be free to move (molten or dissolved) for the compound to conduct.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think electrons flow through the electrolyte.
misconceptions.right: In fact the current in the electrolyte is carried by moving ions. Electrons flow only in the wires and electrodes.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think positive ions go to the positive electrode.
misconceptions.right: In fact opposite charges attract: positive ions go to the negative cathode and negative ions go to the positive anode.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think any solution is an electrolyte.
misconceptions.right: In fact only solutions containing ions are electrolytes. A solution of a covalent substance such as sugar does not conduct.

realWorld: Electrolysis is used to extract reactive metals such as aluminium from their ores.
Electroplating uses electrolysis to coat objects with a thin layer of metal, such as silver or chromium, to protect or decorate them.
The electrolysis of brine (sodium chloride solution) produces chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide for making bleach, plastics and soap.
higherTier: At the cathode positive ions gain electrons (reduction); at the anode negative ions lose electrons (oxidation).
Throughout electrolysis (4.4.3), Higher tier students should be able to write half equations for the reactions at the electrodes, for example Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na and 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.
examTips: Use 'free to move' when explaining why molten or dissolved ionic compounds conduct. 'Free electrons' is wrong for ionic compounds.
Remember PANIC: Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode.
Say that ions are 'attracted' to the oppositely charged electrode.
When asked for products, the metal (or hydrogen) forms at the cathode and the non-metal forms at the anode.
Do not say ions 'carry electrons through the solution'; say the current is carried by moving ions.
summary: Electrolysis splits an ionic compound using electricity.
The compound must be molten or dissolved so ions are free to move.
Cations move to the negative cathode; anions move to the positive anode.
Ions are discharged at the electrodes to form elements.
Inert electrodes (graphite or platinum) are often used.
Current is carried by ions in the electrolyte and by electrons in the wires.

questions.question: What is an electrolyte?
options: A liquid or solution containing ions that are free to move
A metal rod that carries current into a solution
A solution of a covalent compound
markScheme: 1 mark: a liquid or solution containing ions free to move
questions.explanation: An electrolyte conducts because it contains mobile ions. A metal rod is an electrode, and covalent solutions contain no ions.

questions.question: What is the name of the negative electrode in electrolysis?
markScheme: 1 mark: cathode
questions.explanation: The cathode is negative and the anode is positive (PANIC: Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode). The electrolyte is the liquid, not an electrode.

questions.question: During electrolysis, which electrode do positive ions move towards?
markScheme: 1 mark: the negative electrode (cathode)
questions.explanation: Opposite charges attract, so positive ions move to the negative cathode. Positive ions are repelled by the positive anode.

questions.question: Why does solid sodium chloride not conduct electricity?
options: Its ions are fixed in the lattice and cannot move
markScheme: 1 mark: ions fixed in position / cannot move
questions.explanation: Sodium chloride is ionic and does contain ions, but in a solid they are held in place by strong electrostatic forces. It is not covalent, and conduction in ionic compounds depends on ions, not electrons.

questions.question: Which of these is an electrolyte?
markScheme: 1 mark: molten potassium iodide
questions.explanation: Molten potassium iodide has mobile K⁺ and I⁻ ions. The solid has ions that cannot move, sugar solution has no ions, and copper conducts by delocalised electrons so it is a conductor but not an electrolyte.

questions.question: What happens when an ion is discharged at an electrode?
options: It moves back into the electrolyte
It gains or loses electrons to form a neutral atom or molecule
It changes from a positive ion to a negative ion
It reacts with the electrode to form a compound
markScheme: 1 mark: gains or loses electrons to become a neutral atom or molecule
questions.explanation: Discharge means the ion loses its charge by gaining or losing electrons, forming an element. With inert electrodes there is no reaction with the electrode.

questions.question: Molten lead bromide is electrolysed. Towards which electrode do the bromide ions move, and why?
options: The anode, because bromide ions are negative and are attracted to the positive electrode
The cathode, because bromide ions are negative and are attracted to the negative electrode
The anode, because bromide ions are positive
The cathode, because bromine is a non-metal
markScheme: 1 mark: the anode, because Br⁻ is negative and attracted to the positive electrode
questions.explanation: Bromide ions are Br⁻, so they are attracted to the positive anode. Like charges repel, so they are not attracted to the cathode.

questions.question: Why are graphite electrodes often used in electrolysis?
options: Graphite reacts with the products to help them form
Graphite conducts electricity and is inert
markScheme: 1 mark: conducts electricity and is inert (unreactive)
questions.explanation: Graphite has delocalised electrons so it conducts, and it does not usually react with the electrolyte or products. It is a non-metal, not an insulator.

questions.question: Which row correctly describes what carries the electric current in each part of an electrolysis circuit?
markScheme: 1 mark: wires: electrons; electrolyte: ions
questions.explanation: Metals conduct by delocalised electrons. In the electrolyte there are no free electrons, so the current is carried by ions moving to the electrodes.

questions.question: A molten compound XY is electrolysed. Element X forms at the cathode. What can be concluded?
options: X forms positive ions, so X is a metal (or hydrogen)
markScheme: 1 mark: X forms positive ions (metal or hydrogen)
questions.explanation: Only positive ions are attracted to the negative cathode, and positive ions are formed by metals (and hydrogen). Negative ions, from non-metals, go to the anode.

questions.question: State the name of the positive electrode in electrolysis.
markScheme: 1 mark: anode
questions.explanation: The anode is connected to the positive terminal of the power supply.

questions.question: What is meant by electrolysis?
acceptedAnswers: breaking down an ionic compound using electricity
decomposing a molten or dissolved ionic compound with an electric current
markScheme: 1 mark: breaking down (decomposing) an ionic compound, molten or in solution, using an electric current
questions.explanation: Electrolysis uses electrical energy to split an electrolyte into elements.

questions.question: Give two ways of making the ions in an ionic compound free to move.
markScheme: 1 mark: melt it (heat until molten)
1 mark: dissolve it in water
questions.explanation: Both break up the rigid lattice so the ions can move, which lets the compound conduct electricity.

questions.question: Explain why molten sodium chloride conducts electricity but solid sodium chloride does not.
acceptedAnswers: ions free to move when molten
ions fixed in lattice when solid
markScheme: 1 mark: in the solid the ions are held in a fixed position in the lattice / cannot move
1 mark: when molten the ions are free to move and can carry the charge (current)
questions.explanation: Conduction in an ionic compound needs charged particles that can move. Melting overcomes the forces holding the ions in place.

questions.question: Molten magnesium oxide contains Mg²⁺ ions and O²⁻ ions. State which electrode each ion moves to during electrolysis.
markScheme: 1 mark: Mg²⁺ ions move to the cathode (negative electrode)
1 mark: O²⁻ ions move to the anode (positive electrode)
questions.explanation: Mg²⁺ is positive so it is attracted to the negative cathode. O²⁻ is negative so it is attracted to the positive anode.

questions.question: Explain why the ions in an electrolyte move towards the electrodes when a current is switched on.
markScheme: 1 mark: the electrodes are charged / oppositely charged ions are attracted
1 mark: positive ions to the negative electrode and negative ions to the positive electrode
questions.explanation: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged particles pulls each ion towards the electrode with the opposite charge.

questions.question: A solution of sugar in water does not conduct electricity. Explain why.
markScheme: 1 mark: sugar is a covalent (molecular) substance
1 mark: so the solution contains no ions (no charged particles free to move)
questions.explanation: Electrolytes need mobile ions. Sugar molecules are neutral, so dissolving sugar does not produce ions.

questions.question: Describe what happens to positive ions at the cathode and negative ions at the anode in terms of electrons, and name each type of change.
markScheme: 1 mark: positive ions gain electrons at the cathode
1 mark: negative ions lose electrons at the anode
1 mark: gaining electrons is reduction and losing electrons is oxidation
questions.explanation: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain of electrons. Reduction always happens at the cathode and oxidation at the anode.

questions.question: State the type of electrical supply needed for electrolysis.
markScheme: 1 mark: direct current (d.c.)
questions.explanation: A d.c. supply keeps one electrode positive and the other negative, so ions move steadily in one direction.

questions.question: Molten zinc chloride, ZnCl₂, is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Name the product at the cathode and the product at the anode.
markScheme: 1 mark: cathode: zinc
1 mark: anode: chlorine
questions.explanation: Zn²⁺ ions are attracted to the cathode and form zinc metal. Cl⁻ ions are attracted to the anode and form chlorine gas.

questions.question: A student writes: 'In electrolysis, electrons flow through the electrolyte from one electrode to the other.' Explain why this statement is incorrect.
acceptedAnswers: current in electrolyte carried by ions
markScheme: 1 mark: in the electrolyte the current is carried by moving ions (not electrons)
1 mark: electrons flow only through the external circuit (wires and electrodes)
questions.explanation: Electrolytes have no free electrons. Ions carry charge to the electrodes, where electrons are transferred, and electrons then travel round the external wires.

questions.question: When ions are discharged at the electrodes during electrolysis, what type of substance is produced?
markScheme: 1 mark: elements
questions.explanation: Discharging the ions of a compound gives the elements it was made from, such as a metal and a non-metal.

questions.question:
Molten lithium bromide, LiBr, is electrolysed using graphite electrodes.
Describe and explain what happens during the electrolysis. Include why the lithium bromide must be molten, the movement of ions and the products formed at each electrode.
markScheme: Indicative content: lithium bromide is ionic, made of Li⁺ and Br⁻ ions; in the solid the ions are fixed in a lattice and cannot move; when molten the ions are free to move so it conducts (it is an electrolyte); the cathode is negative and the anode is positive; graphite electrodes are inert and conduct; Li⁺ ions are attracted to the cathode; Br⁻ ions are attracted to the anode; at the cathode Li⁺ ions gain electrons and form lithium metal; at the anode Br⁻ ions lose electrons and form bromine; ions are discharged; the compound is decomposed into its elements.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed and correct explanation of why the compound must be molten, the movement of both ions to the correct electrodes, and both products, with reasons.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct movement of ions and at least one product, with some explanation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple relevant statements, for example lithium forms or ions move.
0 marks: nothing worthy of credit.
questions.explanation: The key ideas are mobile ions, attraction of oppositely charged ions to each electrode, and discharge to form lithium at the cathode and bromine at the anode.

questions.question: Explain, in terms of structure and bonding, why ionic compounds can conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water but not when solid.
markScheme: Indicative content: ionic compounds have a giant lattice of positive and negative ions; held by strong electrostatic forces of attraction in all directions; in the solid the ions are fixed and can only vibrate, so they cannot carry charge; melting or dissolving breaks up the lattice (overcomes the forces); the ions are then free to move; moving charged ions carry the current, so the liquid or solution is an electrolyte.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear explanation linking the lattice and strong forces to fixed ions in the solid, and mobile ions carrying charge when molten or dissolved.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states ions cannot move in the solid or can move when molten, with limited explanation.
0 marks: nothing worthy of credit. Answers referring to moving electrons in ionic compounds do not gain credit for that point.
questions.explanation: Conduction needs mobile charged particles. In ionic compounds these are ions, and they become mobile only once the lattice is broken up by melting or dissolving.

questions.question: What is the anode in electrolysis?
markScheme: 1 mark: the positive electrode
questions.explanation: The anode is connected to the positive terminal of the d.c. supply and attracts negative ions.

questions.question: Which statement about the electrode reactions in electrolysis is correct?
options: Positive ions gain electrons at the anode
Negative ions gain electrons at the anode
Negative ions lose electrons at the anode
Positive ions lose electrons at the cathode
markScheme: 1 mark: negative ions lose electrons at the anode
questions.explanation: Negative ions are attracted to the anode and lose their extra electrons (oxidation). Positive ions go to the cathode and gain electrons (reduction).
